                                      PROJECT NO. 58000


 RULEMAKING TO UPDATE                             §       PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 WHOLESALE AND IOU RETAIL
 TRANSMISSION COST RECOVERY IN                    §
 THE ERCOT REGION                                 §                    OF TEXAS
                                                  §


 STACK INFRASTRUCTURE COMMENTS TO PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION IN
                       PROJECT NO. 58000

Introduction:

STACK Infrastructure (“STACK”) appreciates the Commission’s diligent efforts to ensure that
transmission costs associated with new large loads are not shifted to existing residential and
small business customers. STACK also supports a balanced framework that protects ratepayers
while preserving Texas as a competitive and attractive market for technology investment and
enabling the United States and Texas to remain global leaders in artificial intelligence
deployment.

Data center investment delivers significant economic and tax benefits to Texas and its local
communities when developed responsibly with proper safeguards in place, but the magnitude of
such investment requires a high degree of contractual and regulatory certainty, particularly with
respect to access to transmission service.

STACK’s supports the principle that other customer classes should not subsidize large load
customers. As a result, it’s important to ensure the right processes are in place to protect
ratepayers when new significant transmission infrastructure is built to serve large loads. At the
same time, substantial financial commitments should be accompanied by proportionate and
dependable rights to transmission capacity. When a large load customer funds or contractually
commits to pay for firm transmission capacity, that capacity should remain available to the
customer so long as the customer continues to satisfy its financial obligations.

Accordingly, STACK recommends that Project Nos. 58481 and 58000 be considered together.
The two proceedings should establish a coordinated framework that appropriately mitigates
stranded-asset and cost-shifting risks while providing large load customers with the certainty
necessary to make long-term investments in Texas. The framework should include the following
key elements:
    1. Customer Funds Dedicated Interconnection Facilities: Large load customers would
      pay applicable Contributions In Aid of Construction (CIAC) for dedicated
      interconnection facilities.
   2. Financial Security for Network Upgrades: Large load customers would provide
      financial security for network upgrades by providing collateral based on two years of
      minimum bills.
   3. Minimum Demand Charges At Load Ramp Levels: Large load customers should pay
      minimum charges for load levels mutually agreed upon with the interconnecting TSP or
      DSP, subject to concurrent delays in the start of minimum billing for any delays to the
      load ramp caused by forces outside of the customers’ control. Minimum charges should
      be based on a customer’s contract capacity and any consumption in excess of contracted
      capacity should be treated as non-firm curtailable load.
   4. Firm Transmission Capacity Reservation: In return for the above customer
      commitments, the Commission, ERCOT, and TSP or DSP would ensure that the
      contracted capacity remains firm and available so long as the customer satisfies its
      financial and contractual obligations, including through revisions to current TSP and DSP
      form agreements.



STACK also recommends that existing customers with executed agreements have the ability to
opt into the framework adopted by the Commission, allowing them to receive the same rights
and obligations.

Item 1: Customer Funds Dedicated Interconnection Facilities

Large load customers should pay applicable CIAC for dedicated facilities required to serve
customer’s interconnection. CIAC should be limited to facilities constructed solely to serve the
specific customer’s needs. Costs associated with shared network upgrades that provide broader
system benefits should not be funded through an upfront CIAC payment but instead should be
addressed through the minimum billing and financial security framework.

STACK recommends eliminating duplicative definitions in 58481 and 58000. Where the same
concept is addressed in both proceedings, the term should be defined in one place and used
consistently throughout. STACK further recommends using the term “direct interconnection
cost,” as defined in Project No. 58481, because it is more intuitive and descriptive than
“transmission interconnection cost.”

   •   Proposed Redlines to 58481
       §25.194 (f) (9) Contribution in aid of construction (CIAC). A large load customer must
       pay all direct interconnection costs through CIAC, with no standard or other allowance
       offered to offset the customer’s CIAC payments. A large load customer must pay CIAC
        not later than the date that the interconnection agreement is executed. An interconnecting
       DSP and interconnecting TSP must not begin construction of facilities to interconnect a
       large load customer before a large load customer pays CIAC in an amount that is equal to
       the direct interconnection costs associated with the large load customer.

               (A) Direct interconnection costs include all costs associated with facilities built to
               interconnect the large load customer to the existing ERCOT system, including
               radial lines and substation upgrades necessary to interconnect the new large load
               customer. CIAC must be paid in the form of a direct cash payment.

   •   Proposed Redlines to 58000
       §25.192 (b) (13) Transmission Direct interconnection costs -- all costs associated with
       facilities built to interconnect the large load customer to the existing ERCOT system,
       including radial lines and substation upgrades necessary to interconnect the new large load
       customer.
       All costs associated with the facilities required to physically interconnect or upgrade the
       interconnection of a transmission-level customer, or a distinct set of transmission-level
       customers, to the existing transmission network, including interconnection lines, substation
       additions or modifications, and associated equipment necessary to establish or modify
       service.

       §25.252 (b)(5) Transmission Direct interconnection costs. All costs associated with
       the facilities required to physically interconnect or upgrade the interconnection of a
       transmission-level customer, or a distinct set of transmission-level customers, to the
       existing transmission network, including interconnection lines, substation additions or
       modifications, and associated equipment necessary to establish or modify service. Refer
       to 25.192(b) (13).

       §25.252 (c)(2) Contribution in aid of construction. A large load customer must pay
       contribution in aid of construction in accordance with §25.194 of this title (relating to Large
       Load Interconnection Standards).
       (i)    A large load customer must pay contribution in aid of construction for transmission
       interconnection costs and distribution interconnection costs.
       (ii)   Contribution in aid of construction must be made in the form of a direct cash
       payment.
       (iii) An allowance for contribution in aid of construction is prohibited.

Item 2: Financial Security for Network Upgrades

Large load customers should provide financial security for significant equipment purchases and
network upgrade costs attributable to their projects. The amount, duration, and refundability of the
 security should reflect the specific costs and risks being secured and should be coordinated with
CIAC and minimum billing requirements to prevent duplicative recovery or over collection. Many
regions have adopted large load tariffs with a minimum billing framework to ensure recovery of
network upgrades and ensure that other rate classes do not subsidize large load customers. Several
of these frameworks require financial security in the amount of two years of minimum payment
obligations. STACK would be supportive of a similar financial security approach, in addition to
the initial $50,000/MW requirement proposed in 58481.


   •   Proposed Redlines to 58481
       §25.194 (d)(10) Financial security on a dollar per MW basis. Financial security under
       this subsection is due at the time that the intermediate agreement is executed. A large
       load customer must post financial security with the interconnecting DSP or the
       interconnecting TSP in the amount of $50,000 per MW of the requested peak demand for
       new interconnection requests or of the incremental increase in the peak demand for
       expanded interconnection requests.

       (f)(7) Non-refundable interconnection fee. A large load customer must pay an
       interconnection fee in the amount of $50,000 per MW of contracted peak demand. An
       interconnection fee under this subsection is non-refundable.
           a. (f)(7)(A) An interconnecting DSP or an interconnecting TSP must draw on any
               unused financial security that the large load customer posted under an
               intermediate agreement to satisfy the interconnection fee under this subsection.
           b. (f)(7)(B) An interconnection fee under this subsection must be paid to the
               interconnecting TSP and applied by that TSP as an offset to the interconnecting
               TSP’s rate base in the earlier of the interconnecting TSP’s next interim rate
               proceeding or comprehensive rate proceeding.

       (f)(8) Financial security for significant equipment or services. A large load customer
       must post financial security for significant equipment or services not later than the date
       that the interconnection agreement is executed if the interconnecting DSP or the
       interconnecting TSP needs to procure significant equipment or services to interconnect
       the large load customer. An interconnecting DSP and an interconnecting TSP must not
       procure equipment or services before a large load customer posts financial security to the
       interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP in an amount equal to the
       interconnecting DSP and interconnecting TSP’s estimated costs for equipment with a
       lead time of at least six months and services necessary to interconnect the large load
       customer.
        (f)(10) Financial security for system upgrades. A large load customer must post
       financial security for system upgrades that are necessary to reliably serve the large load
       customer at the time of energization (or at the time the capacity is available) not later than
       the date that the interconnection agreement is executed. The amount should be equal to
       the first two years of minimum monthly bills. Security would be released at the end of
       the initial term of the minimum billing contract.

       (h)(4) After applying the financial security to any outstanding amounts owed and
       refunding 20% of the balance, the remaining 80% of the balance must be paid to the
       interconnecting TSP and applied by that TSP as an offset to the interconnecting TSP’s
       rate base in the earlier of the interconnecting TSP’s next interim rate proceeding or
       comprehensive rate proceeding.

Item 3: Minimum Demand Charges At Load Ramp Levels

Large load customers should begin paying minimum billing obligations once the contracted
transmission capacity is available for service according to the agreed-to load ramp between the
large load customer and the interconnecting TSP or DSP. However, a delay in the start of
minimum billing obligations and the phases of the load ramp should be allowed for events that
are outside the large load customers control, such as Force Majeure events or delays in
energization caused by the interconnecting TSP or DSP. In addition, minimum billing
obligations should be based on the contracted capacity according to the agreed to load ramp and
no higher. If a customer is exceeding their contract capacity, the utility should have the ability to
notice the customer to reduce their load, and if the customer does not comply, the utility will
have the right to curtail the customer’s load to get it below its contract capacity.

   •   Proposed Redlines to 58000
       (d) Large load minimum billing demand.
              (1) A REP serving a large load customer, as determined by §25.194 of this title
              (relating to Large Load Interconnection Standards), must be charged for that
              customer based upon a minimum billing demand.
              (2) The minimum billing demand for a large load customer under paragraph (1) of
              this subsection must be the greater of:
                      (A)    the large load customer’s contracted peak demand, as defined in
                             §25.194 of this title (relating to Large Load Interconnection
                             Standards);
                      (B)    the highest non-coincident peak demand placed by the large load
                             customer on the system in the past year; or
                      (C)    the large load customer’s 12CP demand consistent with the most
                             recent ERCOT 12CP intervals, as defined in §25.192 of this title
                             (relating to Transmission Service Rates).
               (3) A large load customer’s billing under this section must commence at the level
              of available service at the time it is available and must be based on the applicable
              agreed upon ramp milestone, up to the amount of capacity then available,
              irrespective of whether the large load customer has energized or is fully using
              available capacity, and for a period of no less than 20 years. Delays to the start of
              billing and phases of the load ramp may be allowed for a force majeure event that
              impedes the customer, interconnecting TSP or DSP from meeting the agreed upon
              ramp milestone.


Item 4: Firm Transmission Capacity Reservation

In return for satisfying these financial obligations, large load customers should retain the
transmission capacity for which they have paid, secured, or contractually committed to pay. The
Commission, ERCOT, and interconnection TSP or DSP should not reduce, reallocate, or claw
back contracted capacity so long as the customer remains in compliance with its applicable
CIAC, financial security, and minimum billing obligations. This reciprocal commitment is
necessary to provide large industrial customers with the certainty required to make substantial,
long-term investments in Texas.

   •   Proposed Redlines to 58481
   25.194 (h) Non-utilized capacity.

       (1) Not later than 30 days after a large load customer fails, by 6 months, to satisfy a
       milestone in its schedule for phased energization, the interconnecting DSP or the
       interconnecting TSP must notify ERCOT of the large load customer’s non-utilized
       capacity.

       (2) Within 60 days of providing notice to ERCOT under this subsection, the
       interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP must draw down on the large load
       customer’s financial security and apply the financial security to any outstanding amounts
       owed. Outstanding amounts owed include the following:

              (A) costs incurred by the interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP to
              fulfill the large load customer’s request for interconnection;

              (B) costs for equipment that the interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP
              procured and that cannot be canceled with a full refund;

              (C) costs for construction that the interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP
              started and that cannot be canceled with a full refund; and

              (D) costs for services that the interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP
              initiated and that cannot be canceled with a full refund.
     (3) Within 60 days of providing notice to ERCOT under this subsection and after
    applying the large load customer’s financial security to any outstanding amounts owed,
    the interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP must refund 20% of the balance to
    the large load customer.

    (4) After applying the financial security to any outstanding amounts owed and refunding
    20% of the balance, the remaining 80% of the balance must be paid to the interconnecting
    TSP and applied by that TSP as an offset to the interconnecting TSP’s rate base in the
    earlier of the interconnecting TSP’s next interim rate proceeding or comprehensive rate
    proceeding.

    (5) CIAC is not refundable.

    (6) ERCOT must reallocate non-utilized capacity.

•   Proposed Redlines to 58000

25.252(c)

    (1) Reservation of transmission capacity. A large load customer must meet the
    following requirements to reserve transmission capacity:

             (A)      execute an interconnection agreement that complies with the requirements
             of §25.194 of this title (relating to Large Load Interconnection Standards);
             (B)      meet the financial commitments and obligations required by §25.194 of this
             title (relating to Large Load Interconnection Standards); and
             (D)      remain in compliance with the interconnection agreement executed in
             accordance with §25.194 of this title (relating to Large Load Interconnection
             Standards).
    (2)      Reallocation. Transmission capacity may be reallocated if a large load customer
    fails to meet the requirements described in this subsection. Transmission capacity may not
    be reallocated if a large load customer meets and continues to meet the financial
    requirements described in this subsection.
 STACK responses to Commission questions in 58000:

   1. Should the values associated with the large load minimum billing demand provisions be
      different for large load customers with different contracted peak demands or different
      non-coincident (NCP) demands

   STACK Response: The same minimum billing methodology should apply to all large
   loads. A uniform framework is simpler to administer, avoids arbitrary size thresholds,
   and provides consistent cost-causation treatment.

   STACK’s position is supportive of comments filed by the Data Center Coalition.

   2. Should the large load minimum billing demand be:
         a. fixed for 20 years as proposed;
         b. reduced in phases over a period of 20 years; or
         c. extended to a longer time period?
   STACK Response: STACK recommends replacing proposed 100%, 20-year minimum
   billing requirement with a data-driven framework that ensures full recovery of transmission
   costs without over-collecting or shifting costs to other customer classes. The minimum
   billing obligation should be based on actual cost of service and apply only to transmission
   capacity that has been constructed and made available to customers.

   STACK’s position is supportive of comments filed by the Data Center Coalition.

   3. Should the large load minimum billing demand be based on some measure of demand
      lower than contracted peak demand and NCP demand? For example, should the large
      load minimum billing demand:

          a. reflect a “ratcheted” demand, wherein the large load minimum billing demand is
             some percentage of the customer’s contracted peak demand or maximum NCP
             demand in the previous year? If so, should the ratchet percentage decline in
             phases over the years, and how?

          b. be based on a “weighted average” minimum billing demand, wherein the large
             load minimum billing demand is some weighted average of the large load
             customer’s contracted peak demand or highest NCP demand over the previous
             year and the large load customer’s 12CP demand? If so, should the percentage
             weighting towards contracted peak demand or NCP demand decline in phases
             over the years, and how?

      STACK Response: Minimum billing demand should always be based on contracted
      capacity so long as the customer intends to reserve the contracted capacity and continues
      to meet its financial obligations. A minimum billing demand that varies based on actual
    demand would potentially minimize the benefits of a minimum billing framework –
   which is to ensure a consistent revenue stream from large load customers independent of
   the fluctuations in demand usage and ensure other rate classes are not subsidizing
   infrastructure caused by large load.

4. Should separate rate treatment be applied to a large computational load, defined as an
   entity that is subject to §25.194 of this title (relating to Large Load Interconnection
   Standards) and in which 50% or greater of the demand at the site consists of power
   electronic based load, specifically computational load, such as data centers and
   cryptocurrency mining facilities? Responses to this question should include applicable
   legal support or limitations regarding separate rate treatment for large computational
   loads.

   STACK Response: STACK’s position is supportive of comments filed by the Data
   Center Coalition.

5. Should the definition for transmission interconnection costs be broadened to include
   transmission projects that are recommended at the conclusion of a batch study to serve
   the transmission capacity needs of a particular load.

   STACK Response: No. CIAC should remain limited to facilities directly and exclusively
   attributable to the customer, such as a dedicated radial interconnection. Shared network
   upgrades should be recovered through the minimum billing framework. Broadening
   CIAC while also imposing minimum billing obligations would create duplicative
   recovery and discourage large-scale investment.

   STACK’s position is supportive of comments filed by the Data Center Coalition.

6. If a large load customer is able to reserve transmission capacity irrespective of whether
   the large load customer has energized or is fully using available capacity, how should
   these loads be reflected in the resource adequacy reports and assessments and
   transmission planning studies?

   STACK Response: Large load customers have every intention of utilizing the load it is
   contracting for. However, there may be factors outside of the customer’s control that
   may make full utilization of its contract capacity challenging for temporary reasons.
   However, since customers will be financially committed under a minimum billing
   construct, the full contract capacity, in accordance with any agreed to load ramp with the
   interconnecting TSP or DSP, should be modeled for resource adequacy reports and
   transmission planning studies.

   STACK’s position is supportive of comments filed by the Data Center Coalition.
 Conclusion:

STACK supports meaningful financial commitments that protect existing customers and ensure
utility cost recovery. In return, the final rule should provide firm capacity rights, align billing
with delivered capacity, avoid duplicative recovery, and establish technically supported
minimum billing demand percentage and term. This balanced framework will protect ratepayers
while sustaining the investment needed to support Texas' continued economic growth.



                                                      Respectfully Submitted,

                                                      Kevin Hughes

                                                      Chief External Affairs Officer

                                                      STACK Americas
                                                      khughes@stackinfra.com
     EXECUTIVE SUMMARY FOR STACK INFRASTRUCTURE COMMENTS TO
           PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION IN PROJECT NO. 58000

STACK Infrastructure (“STACK”) supports the Commission’s efforts to ensure that transmission
costs associated with new large loads are not shifted to residential customers, small businesses,
or other existing ratepayers. Large load customers should bear the costs and financial risks
attributable to their interconnection requests. At the same time, the significant capital
commitments required to develop data centers and other large industrial projects depend on clear,
durable, and enforceable rights to transmission service. When a customer pays for, secures, or
contractually commits to pay for firm transmission capacity, that capacity should remain
available so long as the customer continues to satisfy its financial obligations.

STACK recommends the following framework:

   1. Pay contribution in aid of construction for dedicated interconnection facilities.
      CIAC should apply to customer specific facilities that would not otherwise be constructed
      but for the customer’s request, such as dedicated radial lines and interconnection-specific
      substation facilities. Shared network upgrades that provide broader system benefits
      should not be funded entirely through upfront CIAC payments. Language in §25.192,
      §25.194, and §25.252 should be coordinated to minimize duplication. Defined terms and
      substantive requirements should be established in a single provision and incorporated into
      the other sections by cross-reference.
   2. Provide financial security for network upgrades based on two years of minimum
      bills which many other states have begun to adopt.
      STACK recommends a risk-based security requirement tied to two years of minimum
      demand charges, in addition to the initial $50,000/MW interconnection commitment, to
      provide meaningful collateral for network upgrade costs.
   3. Begin minimum billing as contracted capacity becomes available.
      Minimum billing obligations should commence at the level of transmission service made
      available to the customer. Delays should be permitted when energization is prevented by
      force majeure or by circumstances outside the customer’s control. Minimum billing
      should be based on contracted capacity, should not exceed contracted capacity and should
      not ratchet down over time.
   4. Receive enforceable rights to the capacity supported by those payments.
      The Commission, ERCOT, and transmission service providers should not reduce, claw
      back, or reallocate contracted capacity while the customer remains in compliance with its
      CIAC, financial security, and minimum billing obligations. Reallocation should be
      available only when a customer fails to meet those requirements. Accordingly, STACK
      recommends deleting proposed §25.194(h), which would require ERCOT to reallocate
      capacity after a customer falls six months behind its phased energization schedule, even if
      the customer continues to satisfy its financial obligations.

       interconnecting DSP and interconnecting TSP's estimated costs for equipment with a
       lead time of at least six months and services necessary to interconnect the large load
       customer.
        (f)(10) Financial security for system upgrades. A large load customer must post
       financial security for system upgrades that are necessary to reliably serve the large load
       customer at the time of energization (or at the time the capacity is available) not later than
       the date that the interconnection agreement is executed. The amount should be equal to
       the first two years of minimum monthly bills. Security would be released at the end of
       the initial term of the minimum billing contract.

       (h)(4) After applying the financial security to any outstanding amounts owed and
       refunding 20% of the balance, the remaining 80% of the balance must be paid to the
       interconnecting TSP and applied by that TSP as an offset to the interconnecting TSP' s
       rate base in the earlier of the interconnecting TSP' s next interim rate proceeding or
       comprehensive rate proceeding.

Item 3: Minimum Demand Charges At Load Ramp Levels

Large load customers should begin paying minimum billing obligations once the contracted
transmission capacity is available for service according to the agreed-to load ramp between the
large load customer and the interconnecting TSP or DSP. However, a delay in the start of
minimum billing obligations and the phases of the load ramp should be allowed for events that
are outside the large load customers control, such as Force Maj eure events or delays in
energization caused by the interconnecting TSP or DSP. In addition, minimum billing
obligations should be based on the contracted capacity according to the agreed to load ramp and
no higher. If a customer is exceeding their contract capacity, the utility should have the ability to
notice the customer to reduce their load, and if the customer does not comply, the utility will
have the right to curtail the customer' s load to get it below its contract capacity.

Item 4: Firm Transmission Capacity Reservation

In return for satisfying these financial obligations, large load customers should retain the
transmission capacity for which they have paid, secured, or contractually committed to pay. The
Commission, ERCOT, and interconnection TSP or DSP should not reduce, reallocate, or claw
back contracted capacity so long as the customer remains in compliance with its applicable
CIAC, financial security, and minimum billing obligations. This reciprocal commitment is
necessary to provide large industrial customers with the certainty required to make substantial,
long-term investments in Texas.

 STACK responses to Commission questions in 58000:

   1. Should the values associated with the large load minimum billing demand provisions be
      different for large load customers with different contracted peak demands or different
      non-coincident (NCP) demands

   STACK Response: The same minimum billing methodology should apply to all large
   loads. A uniform framework is simpler to administer, avoids arbitrary size thresholds,
   and provides consistent cost-causation treatment.

   STACK's position is supportive of comments filed by the Data Center Coalition.

   2. Should the large load minimum billing demand be:
         a. fixed for 20 years as proposed;
         b. reduced in phases over a period of 20 years; or
         c. extended to a longer time period?

   STACK Response: STACK recommends replacing proposed 100%, 20-year minimum
   billing requirement with a data-driven framework that ensures full recovery of transmission
   costs without over-collecting or shifting costs to other customer classes. The minimum
   billing obligation should be based on actual cost of service and apply only to transmission
   capacity that has been constructed and made available to customers.

   STACK's position is supportive of comments filed by the Data Center Coalition.

   3. Should the large load minimum billing demand be based on some measure of demand
      lower than contracted peak demand and NCP demand? For example, should the large
      load minimum billing demand:

          a. reflect a "ratcheted" demand, wherein the large load minimum billing demand is
             some percentage of the customer' s contracted peak demand or maximum NCP
              demand in the previous year? If so, should the ratchet percentage decline in
              phases over the years, and how?

          b. be based on a "weighted average" minimum billing demand, wherein the large
             load minimum billing demand is some weighted average of the large load
             customer's contracted peak demand or highest NCP demand over the previous
             year and the large load customer' s 12CP demand? If so, should the percentage
             weighting towards contracted peak demand or NCP demand decline in phases
             over the years, and how?

      STACK Response: Minimum billing demand should always be based on contracted
      capacity so long as the customer intends to reserve the contracted capacity and continues
      to meet its financial obligations. A minimum billing demand that varies based on actual
    demand would potentially minimize the benefits of a minimum billing framework -
   which is to ensure a consistent revenue stream from large load customers independent of
   the fluctuations in demand usage and ensure other rate classes are not subsidizing
   infrastructure caused by large load.

4. Should separate rate treatment be applied to a large computational load, defined as an
   entity that is subject to §25.194 of this title (relating to Large Load Interconnection
   Standards) and in which 50% or greater of the demand at the site consists of power
   electronic based load, specifically computational load, such as data centers and
   cryptocurrency mining facilities? Responses to this question should include applicable
   legal support or limitations regarding separate rate treatment for large computational
   loads.
   STACK Response: STACK' s position is supportive of comments filed by the Data
   Center Coalition.

5. Should the definition for transmission interconnection costs be broadened to include
   transmission projects that are recommended at the conclusion of a batch study to serve
   the transmission capacity needs of a particular load.

   STACK Response: No. CIAC should remain limited to facilities directly and exclusively
   attributable to the customer, such as a dedicated radial interconnection. Shared network
   upgrades should be recovered through the minimum billing framework. Broadening
   CIAC while also imposing minimum billing obligations would create duplicative
   recovery and discourage large-scale investment.

   STACK's position is supportive of comments filed by the Data Center Coalition.

6. If a large load customer is able to reserve transmission capacity irrespective of whether
   the large load customer has energized or is fully using available capacity, how should
   these loads be reflected in the resource adequacy reports and assessments and
   transmission planning studies?

   STACK Response: Large load customers have every intention of utilizing the load it is
   contracting for. However, there may be factors outside of the customer' s control that
   may make full utilization of its contract capacity challenging for temporary reasons.
   However, since customers will be financially committed under a minimum billing
   construct, the full contract capacity, in accordance with any agreed to load ramp with the
   interconnecting TSP or DSP, should be modeled for resource adequacy reports and
   transmission planning studies.

   STACK's position is supportive of comments filed by the Data Center Coalition.
 Conclusion:

STACK supports meaningful financial commitments that protect existing customers and ensure
utility cost recovery. In return, the final rule should provide firm capacity rights, align billing
with delivered capacity, avoid duplicative recovery, and establish technically supported
minimum billing demand percentage and term. This balanced framework will protect ratepayers
while sustaining the investment needed to support Texas' continued economic growth.

     EXECUTIVE SUMMARY FOR STACK INFRASTRUCTURE COMMENTS TO
           PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION IN PROJECT NO. 58000

STACK Infrastructure ("STACK") supports the Commission's efforts to ensure that transmission
costs associated with new large loads are not shifted to residential customers, small businesses,
or other existing ratepayers. Large load customers should bear the costs and financial risks
attributable to their interconnection requests. At the same time, the significant capital
commitments required to develop data centers and other large industrial proj ects depend on clear,
durable, and enforceable rights to transmission service. When a customer pays for, secures, or
contractually commits to pay for firm transmission capacity, that capacity should remain
available so long as the customer continues to satisfy its financial obligations.

STACK recommends the following framework:

   1. Pay contribution in aid of construction for dedicated interconnection facilities.
      CIAC should apply to customer specific facilities that would not otherwise be constructed
      but for the customer' s request, such as dedicated radial lines and interconnection-specific
      substation facilities. Shared network upgrades that provide broader system benefits
      should not be funded entirely through upfront CIAC payments. Language in §25.192,
      §25.194, and §25.252 should be coordinated to minimize duplication. Defined terms and
      substantive requirements should be established in a single provision and incorporated into
      the other sections by cross-reference.
   2. Provide financial security for network upgrades based on two years of minimum
      bills which many other states have begun to adopt.
      STACK recommends a risk-based security requirement tied to two years of minimum
      demand charges, in addition to the initial $50,000/MW interconnection commitment, to
      provide meaningful collateral for network upgrade costs.
   3. Begin minimum billing as contracted capacity becomes available.
      Minimum billing obligations should commence at the level of transmission service made
      available to the customer. Delays should be permitted when energization is prevented by
      force majeure or by circumstances outside the customer's control. Minimum billing
      should be based on contracted capacity, should not exceed contracted capacity and should
      not ratchet down over time.
   4. Receive enforceable rights to the capacity supported by those payments.
      The Commission, ERCOT, and transmission service providers should not reduce, claw
      back, or reallocate contracted capacity while the customer remains in compliance with its
      CIAC, financial security, and minimum billing obligations. Reallocation should be
      available only when a customer fails to meet those requirements. Accordingly, STACK
      recommends deleting proposed §25.194(h), which would require ERCOT to reallocate
      capacity after a customer falls six months behind its phased energization schedule, even if
      the customer continues to satisfy its financial obligations.
